title: What was man created from?
ref: at least 8 distinct materials across 24 verses (see full list below)
text: Man's creation is described using at least eight distinct materials or starting points across roughly two dozen verses: water, dust, clay (in several distinct phrasings — sounding clay, sticky clay, clay like pottery, mud), a fluid or drop of seed, a clot, and simply "nothing."
note: The sheer number of distinct phrasings (see the full list below) is itself the point of contention: is this a single process described from different angles across a long ministry — dust as origin, water/fluid as the reproductive stage, clay as a poetic composite, culminating in the clot/lump stages of embryonic development — or is it evidence of independent, loosely-reconciled sayings on the same question, repeated across many contexts without ever being harmonized into one consistent account? Traditional tafsir generally reads these as sequential stages of one unified process (dust → clay → fluid → clot → lump), while critics note that several verses (e.g. "from water" alone, or "from nothing") don't explicitly fit that sequence when read on their own terms.

title: Was Adam forgiven before or after being told to descend from paradise?
text: In Surah 20, Adam disobeys, is then chosen and forgiven by God, and only afterward is told to descend. In Surahs 2 and 7, the descent command is given immediately upon the transgression, with forgiveness described only afterward — reversing the order of the same two events.
note: Classical tafsir generally treats "descend" in these verses as a single decree announced at different narrative moments rather than a strict blow-by-blow timeline, and reads the descent as a change of abode/status rather than a punishment contingent on forgiveness being withheld. Critics argue the plain sequence of each account, taken on its own terms, puts these two events in a different order — forgiveness-then-descent in one telling, descent-then-forgiveness in the other — which is a genuine chronological tension, not just repeated narration.

title: Can Jews and Christians be saved without converting to Islam?
text: One early verse offers salvation to Jews, Christians, and Sabians who believe and do good; later verses are read as narrowing acceptance to Islam specifically.
note: Exegetes disagree sharply on whether the later verses abrogate the earlier one — a live debate in tafsir literature, not a settled question.

title: Is intercession on the Day of Judgment possible, or not?
text: Some verses allow intercession with God's permission; others state plainly that no intercession will be accepted on that day.
note: Classical theology reconciles these by reading the "no intercession" verses as excluding intercession *without* permission — the permission clause is doing a lot of work in that reconciliation.

title: Is alcohol permitted, cautioned against, or forbidden?
text: Across four passages, alcohol goes from being listed as one of God's provisions, to a caution against praying while intoxicated, to "great sin, some benefit," to an outright abomination to avoid.
note: Widely read as a case of gradual revelation (tadrij) — moving a 7th-century Arabian society toward prohibition in stages rather than all at once. Critics read it as the text visibly changing its mind.

title: Were the heavens or the earth created first?
text: One passage describes the earth being created, then the heavens fashioned above it; another describes the heaven built first, the earth "after that."
note: Translators and commentators dispute whether "after that" (thumma) in 79:30 indicates strict chronological sequence or is a rhetorical transition — a genuine linguistic ambiguity, not a simple slip.

title: Did Abraham pray for his father, or disown him?
text: One passage has Abraham promising to ask forgiveness for his father; another has Abraham and his followers explicitly disowning their disbelieving relatives.
note: Commentators generally read 9:114 as clarifying that Abraham's promise was conditional and later withdrawn once his father's disbelief became clear — a resolution some critics find like a patch applied after the fact.

title: Does the Quran teach free will, or predestination?
text: Some verses describe God sending astray or guiding whom He wills; others tell listeners "whoever wills, let him believe" and describe humans as shown the way, "be he grateful or ungrateful."
note: This tension produced entire theological schools within Islam (Qadariyya vs. Jabriyya, and later Ash'ari vs. Mu'tazila positions) — it's a genuine, historically significant fault line in Islamic theology, not a fringe reading.

title: Did a group of young men really sleep for three hundred years?
text: Young men fall asleep in a cave for over three hundred years and wake up unaged, presented as a sign.
note: The "Sleepers of the Cave" story closely parallels the earlier Christian legend of the Seven Sleepers of Ephesus — read by skeptics as borrowed folklore, by traditionalists as confirmation of a shared prophetic account.

title: Where does the sun set?
text: Dhul-Qarnayn travels until he finds the sun setting in a murky spring.
note: Read literally this implies a bounded or flat cosmology; most modern commentators read it as figurative, describing the western horizon as perceived by a traveler.

title: Where does semen come from, anatomically?
text: Semen is described as coming forth from between the backbone and the ribs.
note: A frequent point of dispute — some apologists argue for a defensible reading, most historians of science read it as reflecting period physiology.

title: Do the creation-material verses actually contradict each other?
text: Man is described as created from clay, from nothing, and from a sperm-drop in different passages.
note: Often read as describing different stages of creation rather than competing accounts, though critics argue the wording doesn't always support that reading.

title: Did creation take six days or eight?
text: There is a mathematical discrepancy regarding the time taken for creation.
note:
Six Days: Multiple verses (7:54, 10:3, 11:7) explicitly state the heavens and earth were created in six days.

Eight Days: A detailed breakdown in Surah 41:9–12 sums to eight days: 2 days for the earth, 4 days for its sustenance/mountains, and 2 days for the heavens (2 + 4 + 2 = 8).

The Conflict: Apologists argue the 4-day period includes the initial 2 days, bringing the total back to six. Critics maintain the text presents them as sequential, additive stages, producing a total that contradicts the "six days" claimed elsewhere.

contested_wording.transliteration: fī sittati ayyāmin
contested_wording.gloss: "in six days" — the repeated phrase for the whole creation

contested_wording.gloss: "in two days" — for the seven heavens

title: Did Noah's son drown, or was he saved?
text: One passage says Noah and his family were delivered; another describes his son refusing to board and ending up among the drowned.
note: Commentators dispute whether "family" in 21:76 was meant to include the disbelieving son at all.

title: Was the revelation permitting Muhammad's marriage to Zaynab genuine, or self-serving?
text: After Zayd — Muhammad's freed slave and adopted son — divorces his wife Zaynab, a verse arrives stating that God married her to Muhammad specifically so that believers would have no difficulty marrying the divorced wives of their adopted sons, and that Muhammad had privately concealed what God intended to reveal.
note:
This is not a contradiction between 33:4-5 and 33:37 — the two are consistent with each other: 33:4-5 establishes that adopted sons aren't legally equivalent to biological sons, and 33:37 explicitly presents itself as the real-world precedent demonstrating that same rule, not an unrelated event. Even critical sources acknowledge this directly.

The actual dispute is over authenticity and timing, not logic: citing historian al-Tabari's account, critics argue Muhammad had grown attracted to Zaynab before Zayd's divorce, and that a conveniently-timed revelation supplied religious sanction for a marriage he already wanted — making this a question about whether the revelation was genuine or a self-interested rationalization.

Traditional and modern apologetic responses (e.g. Ibn Kathir, and contemporary writers like Kaleef Karim) reject the Tabari account as a later, unreliable fabrication intended to defame Muhammad, and read the marriage as deliberate divine legislation — using the Prophet's own life, deliberately, to break a deeply entrenched pre-Islamic taboo that could not have been dismantled by mere instruction alone.

contested_wording.transliteration: wa mā ja'ala ad'iyā'akum abnā'akum
contested_wording.gloss: "nor has He made your adopted sons your [real] sons"

contested_wording.transliteration: fa-lammā qaḍā Zaydun minhā waṭaran zawwajnākahā
contested_wording.arabic: فَلَمَّا قَضَىٰ زَيْدٌ مِّنْهَا وَطَرًا زَوَّجْنَاكَهَا
contested_wording.gloss: "so when Zayd had no longer any need for her, We married her to you"

title: What does "strike above the necks" actually instruct?
text: God tells the angels He will cast terror into the hearts of unbelievers, and to strike above the necks and at every fingertip.
note: Tied to the Battle of Badr; most scholars read it as describing a specific engagement, not a standing instruction for all time.

title: What does the "sword verse" actually say — and to whom?
text: Once the sacred months pass, slay the idolaters wherever found, unless they repent and establish prayer.
note: Probably the single most-cited verse in polemics against the Quran. Mainstream scholarship reads it in the context of a specific broken treaty, not a general command — a genuinely contested reading.

title: What punishment does the Quran prescribe for "spreading corruption"?
text: Prescribes execution, crucifixion, or amputation of hands and feet on alternate sides for those who wage war against God and spread corruption in the land.
note: Classical jurisprudence limits this to armed rebellion or brigandage; it's frequently cited independent of that limiting context.

title: What does the Quran say about a husband's authority over his wife?
text: Men are described as having authority over women; persistent disobedience may be addressed by admonition, separation, then a physical measure.
note: One of the most contested verses in the entire text — reformist and traditional translators render the final measure very differently, from a light tap to a strike.

contested_wording.transliteration: wa-ḍribūhunna
contested_wording.gloss: from the root ḍa-ra-ba (ض ر ب), most commonly rendered "strike them" or "beat them"; a minority of modern translators and scholars (e.g. drawing on the idiom "ḍaraba fī al-arḍ," to depart/travel) argue for a reading closer to "leave them" or "separate from them" — a reading most classical and contemporary scholars reject as inconsistent with how the root is used elsewhere in the text

title: Why does a woman's testimony count as half in some verses?
text: In matters of debt, calls for two male witnesses, or one man and two women, "so that if one errs, the other can remind her."
note:
Classical explanation: The dominant classical tafsir (e.g., Ibn Kathir) attributes this directly to a "shortcoming in her mind" (naqṣ fī 'aqlihā) — framing it as a claim about women's comparative reliability in recollection generally, not limited to commercial contexts.

Reformist/contextual explanation: Modern scholars (e.g., Taha Jaber Al-Alwani) reject that reading, arguing the verse instead reflects that business and commercial transactions were overwhelmingly a male domain by social custom in 7th-century Arabia — meaning women in general simply had less everyday exposure to contracts and financial dealings, not that they were less capable. On this reading, a woman experienced in business (a merchant, for instance) would not be subject to the same discount.

The tension: These two explanations disagree with each other, not just with critics — one is about innate ability, the other about social exclusion from a specific domain. Historically, women's broad exclusion from formal commercial and legal training in this period is well documented; whether the verse itself intends that as its reasoning, versus a claim about cognitive difference, remains genuinely disputed among Muslim scholars themselves.

contested_wording.transliteration: an taḍilla iḥdāhumā fa-tudhakkira iḥdāhumā al-ukhrā
contested_wording.arabic: أَن تَضِلَّ إِحْدَاهُمَا فَتُذَكِّرَ إِحْدَاهُمَا الْأُخْرَىٰ
contested_wording.gloss: "lest one of them errs, so the other reminds her" — the verse's own stated reason; it does not itself use language about cognitive shortcoming

contested_wording.ref: Ibn Kathir's tafsir on 2:282 (not a Quranic verse)
contested_wording.transliteration: naqṣun fī 'aqlihā
contested_wording.gloss: "a shortcoming in her mind" — the phrase used in classical commentary to explain the verse, not language appearing in the Quranic text itself

title: What does the "tilth" verse mean?
text: Wives are described using an agricultural metaphor — a "tilth," approached as the husband wishes.
note: Read very differently by different commentators — some as possessive language, others as a statement about intimacy and continuity of family.

title: Does the Quran forbid friendship with Jews and Christians?
text: Believers are told not to take Jews and Christians as allies of one another.
note: Translators disagree heavily on what the underlying term ("awliya") implies — political alliance in a specific wartime setting, versus a blanket social prohibition.

title: What does the Quran say about non-Muslims paying the jizya?
text: Instructs fighting against People of the Book who do not believe as prescribed, until they pay the jizya in submission.
note: Historically the textual basis for the dhimmi system; scholars dispute whether it describes wartime policy or a permanent religious hierarchy.

title: Does the Quran actually say there's no compulsion in religion?
text: There is no compulsion in religion; the right path has become distinct from error.
note: The text argues with itself on the question of religious coercion — this verse sits right alongside the harsher ones above, and deserves equal weight.

title: What does the Quran say about different nations and tribes?
text: Humanity was made into nations and tribes so that people would come to know one another; the most honored are the most righteous.
note: Frequently cited as the Quran's pluralist counterweight — the "know one another" verse, popular in interfaith contexts.

title: What does the Quran say about the value of a single life?
text: Whoever kills a soul unjustly, it is as if he had killed all of mankind, and whoever saves one, it is as if he had saved all of mankind.
note: One of the most widely quoted verses by Muslims themselves, including in public condemnations of terrorism.

title: Does the Quran instruct responding to evil with good?
text: Repel evil with what is better, and the one who was your enemy may become like a close friend.
note: A direct counterpart to the harsher battlefield verses elsewhere in the text — worth reading in the same sitting as those.

title: Was Haman really a minister to Pharaoh?
text: Haman appears repeatedly as a minister in the Egyptian Pharaoh's court during the time of Moses, tasked at one point with building a tower to reach the heavens.
note: Outside the Quran, Haman is a figure from the Book of Esther — a minister to the Persian king Ahasuerus, roughly 900 years after Moses and in a different empire entirely. Some scholars read this as a title or literary echo rather than a strict historical claim, and note the name may have circulated independently in regional storytelling; others see it as a straightforward anachronism carried over from conflating separate traditions.

contested_wording.transliteration: wa Fir'awna wa Hāmāna wa junūdahumā
contested_wording.gloss: "and Pharaoh and Haman and their soldiers" — Haman named directly alongside Pharaoh

contested_wording.transliteration: inna Fir'awna wa Hāmāna wa junūdahumā kānū khāṭi'īn
contested_wording.arabic: إِنَّ فِرْعَوْنَ وَهَامَانَ وَجُنُودَهُمَا كَانُوا خَاطِئِينَ
contested_wording.gloss: "indeed, Pharaoh, Haman, and their soldiers were sinners"

contested_wording.transliteration: yā Hāmānu ibni lī ṣarḥan
contested_wording.gloss: "O Haman, build for me a tower" — Pharaoh's direct command to Haman

contested_wording.transliteration: wa Qārūna wa Fir'awna wa Hāmāna
contested_wording.gloss: "and Korah, and Pharaoh, and Haman" — all three named among those destroyed for arrogance

contested_wording.transliteration: ilā Fir'awna wa Hāmāna wa Qārūn
contested_wording.gloss: "to Pharaoh, Haman, and Korah" — Moses and Aaron sent to all three together

contested_wording.transliteration: wa qāla Fir'awnu yā Hāmānu ibni lī ṣarḥan la'allī ablughu al-asbāb
contested_wording.arabic: وَقَالَ فِرْعَوْنُ يَا هَامَانُ ابْنِ لِي صَرْحًا لَّعَلِّي أَبْلُغُ الْأَسْبَابَ
contested_wording.gloss: "and Pharaoh said, O Haman, build for me a tower so that I may reach the ways" — the fullest version of the tower request, explicitly to "see the God of Moses"

title: Did "the Samaritan" really make the golden calf?
text: A figure called "al-Samiri" ("the Samaritan") is blamed for crafting the golden calf during the Exodus from Egypt.
note: The Samaritan people, and the city of Samaria they're named for, didn't exist until centuries after Moses' era, following the Assyrian conquest of the northern kingdom of Israel. Some commentators propose "al-Samiri" may reflect an unrelated tribal or personal name rather than a reference to Samaritans specifically; the identification remains debated among both classical and modern scholars.

contested_wording.transliteration: wa aḍallahumu as-Sāmiriyy
contested_wording.gloss: "and as-Samiri led them astray"

contested_wording.transliteration: qāla fa-mā khaṭbuka yā Sāmiriyy... qāla baṣurtu bimā lam yabṣurū bihi
contested_wording.arabic: قَالَ فَمَا خَطْبُكَ يَا سَامِرِيُّ ۖ قَالَ بَصُرْتُ بِمَا لَمْ يَبْصُرُوا بِهِ
contested_wording.gloss: "he said, what is your case, O Samiri? He said, I saw what they did not see"

title: Is Mary, mother of Jesus, confused with Miriam, sister of Moses?
text: Mary is addressed as "sister of Aaron" and identified as the daughter of "Imran" (Amram) — names that belong to Moses' sister Miriam and her father, who lived roughly 1,300 years before Mary.
note: Traditional tafsir explains "sister of Aaron" as an honorific for belonging to a priestly lineage (much as an Arabic speaker might call a pious man "brother of so-and-so" without a literal sibling relationship), not a genealogical claim. Critics find this explanation strained given how specifically Imran and Aaron are named elsewhere in the same text.

contested_wording.transliteration: yā ukhta Hārūna mā kāna abūki imra'a saw'in
contested_wording.arabic: يَا أُخْتَ هَارُونَ مَا كَانَ أَبُوكِ امْرَأَ سَوْءٍ
contested_wording.gloss: "O sister of Aaron, your father was not a man of evil"

contested_wording.transliteration: wa Maryama ibnata 'Imrān
contested_wording.gloss: "and Mary, daughter of Imran"

title: Does the Quran accurately describe the Christian Trinity?
text: God asks Jesus whether he told people to take him and his mother as two gods besides God — describing the Trinity as Father, Son, and Mary.
note: No mainstream Christian doctrine, ancient or modern, has ever held Mary as the third person of the Trinity (that role belongs to the Holy Spirit). Some historians propose this reflects a real but marginal sect (such as the Collyridians, a small group reported to have venerated Mary in a god-like role) rather than a description of orthodox Christianity broadly — though whether that group still existed by the 7th century, or was widespread enough to be the intended target, is itself disputed.

title: How long is a day to God — 1,000 years, or 50,000?
text: Two passages describe a day with God as equal to a thousand years; another describes the angels and the Spirit ascending to Him in a day equal to fifty thousand years.
note: Commentators generally read these as describing different things entirely — one about divine timelessness in general, the other specifically about the length of the Day of Judgment — rather than a fixed, contradictory conversion rate. Critics counter that both are still presented as measures of "a day" relative to God, which is where the tension lies.

contested_wording.transliteration: yawman 'inda rabbika ka-alfi sanatin mimmā ta'uddūn
contested_wording.arabic: يَوْمًا عِندَ رَبِّكَ كَأَلْفِ سَنَةٍ مِّمَّا تَعُدُّونَ
contested_wording.gloss: "a day with your Lord is like a thousand years of what you count"

contested_wording.transliteration: fī yawmin kāna miqdāruhu khamsīna alfa sanah
contested_wording.arabic: فِي يَوْمٍ كَانَ مِقْدَارُهُ خَمْسِينَ أَلْفَ سَنَةٍ
contested_wording.gloss: "in a Day the extent of which is fifty thousand years"

title: Does anyone bear the sins of another?
text: Several verses state plainly that no soul bears the burden of another. Elsewhere, Abel tells Cain he wants him to bear both their sins, and other verses describe wrongdoers bearing "their own burdens, and other burdens along with their own."
note: One classical harmonization reads the second set of verses as describing people who bear guilt for *leading others astray*, in addition to their own sin — not literally inheriting someone else's separate wrongdoing. Scholars such as Gabriel Said Reynolds have noted the tension remains genuinely debated in academic Quranic studies, not just polemical literature.

contested_wording.transliteration: wa lā taziru wāziratun wizra ukhrā
contested_wording.gloss: "no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another"

contested_wording.transliteration: innī urīdu an tabū'a bi-ithmī wa ithmik
contested_wording.arabic: إِنِّي أُرِيدُ أَن تَبُوءَ بِإِثْمِي وَإِثْمِكَ
contested_wording.gloss: "I want you to bear my sin and your sin" — Abel to Cain

contested_wording.transliteration: wa la-yaḥmilunna athqālahum wa athqālan ma'a athqālihim
contested_wording.gloss: "they will surely carry their own burdens, and burdens along with their own burdens"

title: Who takes a person's soul at death?
text: One verse describes "the angel of death" (singular) as the one put in charge of taking souls; several other verses describe "angels" (plural) doing the same task.
note: A common harmonization treats this the way a single police chief might command a squad — one angel in overall charge, with subordinate angels carrying out the task — rather than a strict either/or claim. Whether the text itself actually supports that reading, or whether it's a reconciliation applied after the fact, is where critics and traditional exegetes part ways.

contested_wording.transliteration: yatawaffākum malaku al-mawti alladhī wukkila bikum
contested_wording.arabic: يَتَوَفَّاكُم مَّلَكُ الْمَوْتِ الَّذِي وُكِّلَ بِكُمْ
contested_wording.gloss: "the angel of death, who has been put in charge of you, will take your souls" (singular)

contested_wording.transliteration: tatawaffāhumu al-malā'ika
contested_wording.gloss: "the angels take them in death" (plural)

contested_wording.transliteration: tawaffathu rusulunā
contested_wording.gloss: "Our messengers take him" (a third phrasing)

title: Are mountains "pegs" that stabilize the earth?
text: The earth is described as spread out flat with mountains cast into it like pegs (awtad), so that it does not shake with its inhabitants.
note: A popular modern apologetic claim reads this as anticipating isostasy — the idea that mountains have deep roots anchoring them, much like a peg. Geologists and historians of science more commonly read "pegs" as ordinary Late Antique cosmological imagery (mountains as tent-stakes holding down a flat earth), found in comparable form in pre-Islamic Near Eastern texts, rather than a specific geological claim.

contested_wording.transliteration: a-lam naj'ali al-arḍa mihādā, wa al-jibāla awtādā
contested_wording.arabic: أَلَمْ نَجْعَلِ الْأَرْضَ مِهَادًا وَالْجِبَالَ أَوْتَادًا
contested_wording.gloss: "have We not made the earth a resting place, and the mountains as pegs?"

contested_wording.transliteration: wa alqā fī al-arḍi rawāsiya an tamīda bikum
contested_wording.arabic: وَأَلْقَىٰ فِي الْأَرْضِ رَوَاسِيَ أَن تَمِيدَ بِكُمْ
contested_wording.gloss: "He cast into the earth firmly-set mountains, lest it shift with you"

title: Was iron "sent down" from the sky?
text: The verse states that God "sent down iron, in which is great strength and benefits for mankind."
note: A popular apologetic argument connects this to the real astrophysical fact that iron on Earth ultimately originates from supernova nucleosynthesis, framing it as remarkable foreknowledge. Linguists and classical commentators point out that "sent down" (anzalna) is a routine Quranic idiom applied to ordinary provisions — cattle, clothing, and rain are all described the same way — making it a stretch to read this one instance as a specific claim about the interstellar origin of a metal.

title: Do the Quran's embryology verses describe stages unknown before modern science?
text: Human development is described in stages: a drop, then a clinging clot (alaqah), then a chewed-like lump (mudghah), then bones clothed with flesh.
note: This claim gained wide popularity after embryologist Keith Moore endorsed it in a 1980s textbook edition co-produced with Saudi funding — an endorsement that has since been widely criticized by other scientists as promotional rather than an independent scientific assessment. Historians of science note that the staged terminology closely parallels Galenic and Hippocratic embryology already circulating in the 7th-century Near East, predating the Quran by centuries.

contested_wording.transliteration: thumma khalaqnā an-nuṭfata 'alaqatan fa-khalaqnā al-'alaqata muḍghatan
contested_wording.arabic: ثُمَّ خَلَقْنَا النُّطْفَةَ عَلَقَةً فَخَلَقْنَا الْعَلَقَةَ مُضْغَةً
contested_wording.gloss: "then We made the drop into a clinging clot, then We made the clot into a lump"

contested_wording.transliteration: min nuṭfatin thumma min 'alaqatin thumma min muḍghah
contested_wording.arabic: مِن نُّطْفَةٍ ثُمَّ مِنْ عَلَقَةٍ ثُمَّ مِن مُّضْغَةٍ
contested_wording.gloss: the same staged sequence repeated

title: Does the Quran describe an expanding universe?
text: The verse states: "And the heaven We constructed with strength, and indeed, We are expanding it."
note: Popularized as a prediction of Hubble's 1929 discovery of cosmic expansion. Classical tafsir written centuries before that discovery overwhelmingly reads this verse as being about the vastness and power of God's creation in a general sense, not a specific physical claim about the universe's ongoing expansion — the scientific reading only became common well after the relevant discovery had already been made.

title: Why does a daughter inherit half of what a son inherits?
text: In matters of inheritance, a son's share is set equal to that of two daughters.
note: The traditional jurisprudential explanation ties this to classical family law, where men alone bore financial responsibility for the household (mahr, maintenance, inheritance obligations to female relatives), making the shares about differing obligations rather than differing worth. Critics note this reasoning doesn't map cleanly onto modern contexts where women often share or carry equal financial responsibility.

title: What does the Quran say about a man marrying more than one wife?
text: Permits marrying two, three, or four women, "but if you fear you will not be just, then marry only one."
note: The verse's context follows a passage about protecting orphans, and reformist scholars (Muhammad Abduh among the earliest) read the justice condition as a practical restriction pointing toward monogamy as the default. Traditional jurisprudence has more commonly treated it as a general permission with a moral caveat attached, rather than a restriction in practice.

title: Does the Quran itself prescribe a worldly punishment for leaving Islam?
text: Apostates are described as having their deeds rendered worthless, and facing God's wrath and Hellfire — described consistently as a Day of Judgment consequence rather than an earthly one.
note: A common misconception, shared by some critics and some traditional apologists alike, is that the Quran itself commands execution for apostasy. Multiple contemporary scholars (including Mohammad Hashim Kamali and Muhammad Abed al-Jabiri) have argued the Quranic text specifies only otherworldly punishment; the death penalty found in classical Islamic law derives primarily from hadith and juristic reasoning tied to the historical Ridda wars, not a direct Quranic verse — a distinction reformist scholars consider significant, and traditionalist scholars often dispute.

contested_wording.transliteration: wa man yartadid minkum 'an dīnihi fa-yamut wa huwa kāfirun fa-ulā'ika ḥabiṭat a'māluhum
contested_wording.arabic: وَمَن يَرْتَدِدْ مِنكُمْ عَن دِينِهِ فَيَمُتْ وَهُوَ كَافِرٌ فَأُولَٰئِكَ حَبِطَتْ أَعْمَالُهُمْ
contested_wording.gloss: "whoever of you reverts from his religion and dies a disbeliever, their deeds become worthless"

contested_wording.transliteration: man kafara billāhi min ba'di īmānihi... fa-'alayhim ghaḍabun min Allāh
contested_wording.arabic: مَن كَفَرَ بِاللَّهِ مِن بَعْدِ إِيمَانِهِ ... فَعَلَيْهِمْ غَضَبٌ مِّنَ اللَّهِ
contested_wording.gloss: "whoever disbelieves in God after his belief... upon them is wrath from God"

title: What does the Quran say about sexual relations with female captives?
text: Several passages permit sexual relations with wives, "or those whom their right hands possess" — a phrase classical exegetes overwhelmingly identified with female war captives and slaves.
note: Classical commentators (e.g., al-Qurtubi) read this straightforwardly as permitting a master to have relations with an enslaved woman without marriage. A minority of modern reformist scholars argue the phrase has been misread, and that it more narrowly refers to women already lawfully married under the owner's authority, not license for a new sexual relationship — a reading rejected by most classical and many contemporary Islamic jurists as inconsistent with the historical exegetical record.

contested_wording.transliteration: illā 'alā azwājihim aw mā malakat aymānuhum
contested_wording.arabic: إِلَّا عَلَىٰ أَزْوَاجِهِمْ أَوْ مَا مَلَكَتْ أَيْمَانُهُمْ
contested_wording.gloss: "except from their wives or those whom their right hands possess"

contested_wording.transliteration: mā malakat aymānukum
contested_wording.gloss: "what your right hands possess" — the same phrase repeated

title: Did Muhammad briefly recite verses endorsing pagan goddesses, then retract them?
text: Early Islamic historical sources (including al-Tabari and Ibn Ishaq's biography) describe an incident where Muhammad reportedly recited lines granting intercessory power to three Meccan goddesses — Allat, al-Uzza, and Manat — before Gabriel corrected him, explaining Satan had inserted the words.
note: Many later and modern Muslim scholars reject the historicity of the incident entirely, arguing the chain of transmission is weak and the story doesn't fit Muhammad's established prophetic protections from error (isma). Western historians are divided: some treat it as too embarrassing to have been fabricated by later Muslims (an argument from awkwardness), while others agree the sourcing is too weak to support historical confidence either way.

title: Were competing versions of the Quran destroyed to create one standard text?
ref: Historical account, not a Quranic verse
text: Islamic historical sources themselves record that the third caliph, Uthman, ordered a single standardized text compiled and distributed, and commanded that other existing codices — including those associated with companions Ibn Mas'ud and Ubayy ibn Ka'b — be destroyed.
note: This is not a critics' invention; it's recorded approvingly in early Islamic historiography (notably Sahih al-Bukhari) as a necessary act to prevent disputes over recitation, not something scandalous. Some modern scholars nonetheless view it as evidence of real textual variation in the earliest period that was later suppressed rather than organically converging; traditional scholarship treats it as confirmation of the text's careful, deliberate preservation.

title: What did the Sana'a palimpsest reveal about the Quran's early text?
ref: Historical/manuscript evidence, not a Quranic verse
text: A cache of very early Quran parchments discovered in Yemen in 1972 turned out to be a palimpsest — text that had been scraped off and written over — with an undertext differing from the standard Uthmanic text in word order, spelling, and occasionally content.
note: Scholars like Gerd Puin, who studied the manuscript closely, describe it as evidence of a text that was still evolving in its earliest decades. Other scholars, including Muslim researchers who worked on the same manuscript, argue the differences are consistent with known, accepted variant reading traditions (qira'at) rather than evidence of substantive doctrinal instability — a genuinely live academic disagreement, not a fringe claim on either side.

title: Does the Quran treat magic and witchcraft as real, effective forces?
text: Believers are instructed to seek refuge with God from "the evil of those who blow on knots" — a reference to a folk-magic practice of casting spells by tying and blowing on knotted cords.
note: Read literally, this treats knot-magic as a real source of harm requiring supernatural protection, consistent with widespread pre-Islamic Arabian folk belief. Some modern commentators reinterpret this as addressing psychological harm from malicious suggestion or gossip rather than literal sorcery, though this reading departs from how the verse was understood by classical exegetes closer to the time it was revealed.

title: Are shooting stars missiles thrown at eavesdropping devils?
text: Stars are described as adorning the lowest heaven and serving as missiles hurled at devils (jinn) who try to eavesdrop on the angels' assembly, driving them away with a pursuing flame.
note: Some commentators read "shihāb" (translated "missile"/"flame") more broadly as a blaze or flare rather than a literal projectile, softening the mechanical claim. Read plainly, though, the text presents a real causal mechanism — meteors exist specifically to repel eavesdropping spirits — which doesn't correspond to the actual physics of meteoroids burning up on atmospheric entry. The concept closely parallels earlier Jewish and Zoroastrian mythology about stars guarding the heavens, suggesting shared pre-modern cosmology rather than a scientific claim.

contested_wording.transliteration: wa ḥafiẓnāhā min kulli shayṭānin rajīm
contested_wording.gloss: "and We guarded it from every accursed devil"

contested_wording.transliteration: illā man khaṭifa al-khaṭfata fa-atba'ahu shihābun thāqib
contested_wording.arabic: إِلَّا مَنْ خَطِفَ الْخَطْفَةَ فَأَتْبَعَهُ شِهَابٌ ثَاقِبٌ
contested_wording.gloss: "except one who snatches a glimpse, and he is pursued by a piercing flame"

contested_wording.transliteration: wa ja'alnāhā rujūman lish-shayāṭīn
contested_wording.gloss: "and We have made them missiles against the devils"

title: Did Solomon really understand the speech of ants and birds?
text: An ant is described warning other ants to take shelter before Solomon's army unknowingly crushes them; a hoopoe bird later reports back to Solomon with detailed political intelligence about the Queen of Sheba's kingdom.
note: Islamic tradition presents this explicitly as a miracle unique to Solomon (understanding the "speech of birds," mantiq al-tayr, stated directly in 27:16) rather than a claim about ordinary animal cognition — so it isn't offered as a scientific claim to begin with. Critics note the text nonetheless treats these events as literal historical narrative, not allegory, including detailed reported dialogue from the ant and reconnaissance-level detail from the bird.

title: Are there seven physical heavens held up without visible pillars?
text: The heavens are described as seven layers, raised "without pillars that you can see," each containing its own order, with the lowest adorned by stars.
note: A popular modern apologetic reading treats "without pillars you can see" as hinting at invisible physical forces (like gravity) holding celestial bodies in place. Historians of religion more commonly read "seven heavens" as a widely shared cosmological model across the ancient Near East (also found in Babylonian and Jewish sources) describing physical layered domes, not a claim compatible with modern astrophysics, which doesn't describe the universe as seven discrete layers at all.

contested_wording.transliteration: Allāhu alladhī rafa'a as-samāwāti bi-ghayri 'amadin tarawnahā
contested_wording.arabic: اللَّهُ الَّذِي رَفَعَ السَّمَاوَاتِ بِغَيْرِ عَمَدٍ تَرَوْنَهَا
contested_wording.gloss: "God, who raised the heavens without pillars that you can see"

contested_wording.transliteration: khalaqa sab'a samāwātin ṭibāqā
contested_wording.gloss: "created seven heavens in layers"

contested_wording.transliteration: fa-sawwāhunna sab'a samāwāt
contested_wording.gloss: "and fashioned them as seven heavens"

title: Did Dhul-Qarnayn really build a wall of iron and molten copper to contain Gog and Magog?
text: Dhul-Qarnayn is asked to build a barrier against Gog and Magog (Ya'juj wa Ma'juj); he constructs a wall from iron blocks fused together with molten copper, sealing off a mountain pass.
note: Some historians connect this account to real ancient fortifications known to travelers in Late Antiquity, such as the Caspian Gates or the Great Wall of Gorgan in Iran, suggesting the story may echo genuine engineering feats rather than being pure invention. Critics note the wall's function in the text is explicitly eschatological — it holds back Gog and Magog until a divinely appointed end-times release (also referenced in 21:96) — which goes well beyond describing a historical structure and into legendary territory.

title: Was the Queen of Sheba's throne teleported instantly to Solomon?
text: Solomon asks his court who can bring him the Queen of Sheba's throne before she arrives; a jinn offers to bring it before he rises from his seat, but "one who had knowledge of the Scripture" brings it instantly, faster than the blink of an eye.
note: The text explicitly frames this as a supernatural sign ("this is by the favor of my Lord," 27:40), not an ordinary physical claim — so it's presented as miraculous by its own terms, similar to Solomon's other reported abilities in the same narrative. Critics note it's still recounted as literal historical event within the text's narrative logic, involving what amounts to instantaneous long-distance matter transportation, centuries before any physical framework that could account for it.

title: Does the Quran require amputating a thief's hand?
text: Instructs cutting off the hand of a male or female thief as retribution and a deterrent punishment from God, immediately followed by a promise that God forgives whoever repents afterward.
note: Classical scholarship (Ibn Kathir, and the historical case of a woman whose hand was cut off in the Prophet's own time despite an offer of ransom) reads the repentance clause in 5:39 as forgiveness in the *afterlife* sense, not a legal pardon that cancels the earthly punishment — the two are treated as separate tracks. A minority of modern "Quran-alone" reformists argue the Arabic root for "cut" (qata'a) can carry a metaphorical sense (severing someone's means or opportunity to steal again) rather than literal amputation, though this reading is a distinct minority position rejected by both classical and most contemporary scholarship.

title: Does the Quran instruct showing no pity while flogging unmarried people for sex?
text: Instructs 100 lashes for unmarried people found guilty of sexual intercourse, explicitly stating that no pity for them should prevent carrying out the punishment, to be witnessed by a group of believers.
note: Commonly cited in mitigation: the Quran elsewhere (4:15, and this same surah's verse 13) sets an extremely high evidentiary bar — four eyewitnesses to the actual act — making a valid conviction under the letter of the law very rare in practice; some scholars argue this near-impossible standard functions as a practical deterrent against ever actually carrying out the punishment, more than a realistic enforcement mechanism. Critics counter that the explicit "let no pity overcome you" language remains a striking textual instruction regardless of how rarely it could be legally applied.

title: Does the Quran command "an eye for an eye" retaliation?
text: Establishes a law of retaliation (qisas) — a life for a life, an eye for an eye, a wound for a wound — while also stating that whoever forgoes retaliation as charity, it serves as expiation.
note: Widely read by classical and modern scholars alike as a *limiting* reform rather than a harsh innovation — pre-Islamic Arabian custom often involved disproportionate tribal revenge (killing multiple people, or someone of higher status than the original victim, in retaliation for one death), and this law caps retribution at exact proportional equivalence while actively encouraging forgiveness instead. Critics note that whatever its historical improvement over prior custom, the law still codifies literal corporal retaliation (an eye actually being removed) as a default legal option, not merely a metaphor.

contested_wording.transliteration: kutiba 'alaykumu al-qiṣāṣu fī al-qatlā
contested_wording.gloss: "retaliation is prescribed for you in cases of murder"

contested_wording.transliteration: an-nafsa bi-an-nafsi wa al-'ayna bi-al-'ayni
contested_wording.gloss: "a life for a life, an eye for an eye"

title: What does "smite the necks" of unbelievers in battle actually instruct?
text: Instructs believers, upon meeting unbelievers in battle, to smite their necks; once the enemy is subdued, captives are to be bound, then later released either by an act of grace or for ransom, until the war ends.
note: Often cited by commentators (including Qur'an Wiki's analysis) as comparatively restrained for its era — the verse explicitly limits the treatment of captives to only two options, release or ransom, with no mention of execution or enslavement as alternatives, which several scholars read as a real constraint on wartime conduct relative to contemporary norms. Critics note the verse is nonetheless describing literal combat instructions using graphic language (smiting necks, "until you have crushed them"), not a purely defensive or metaphorical framing, and that hadith literature (e.g., "jihad shall continue until the Day of Judgment") extends its application well beyond the immediate historical battle.

title: Does the Quran describe skin being regrown specifically so torment can continue?
text: Describes those who reject God's signs as being burned in Fire; whenever their skin is thoroughly burned, God will replace it with new skin so they may taste the punishment again — described as an expression of God's might and wisdom.
note: Traditional theology frames this as illustrating the totality and justice of divine punishment (Al-'Aziz, Al-Hakim) rather than gratuitous cruelty — sensation and accountability continuing without a merciful end for unrepentant rejection. This is a different genre from the earthly legal punishments elsewhere in this category (a description of the afterlife, not a command directed at believers to carry out), though critics note it's still a deliberately engineered mechanism for perpetuating physical suffering, presented without qualification or limit.

title: Does the Quran instruct believers not to ally with their own fathers and brothers?
text: Instructs believers not to take their fathers or brothers as allies if they prefer disbelief over faith, calling anyone who does so a wrongdoer.
note: Classical and modern commentary (Ma'arif al-Qur'an, and mainstream apologetics) situate this in a specific historical context: early Muslim converts whose own relatives fought against them at Badr and Uhud, where the verse addresses active battlefield allegiance, not ordinary family relations. Other verses (e.g. 31:15) explicitly instruct kindness toward disbelieving parents even while maintaining religious boundaries. Critics note the verse's plain wording is not limited to combat scenarios, and that it has real, documented modern relevance for people who face family estrangement over leaving or questioning the faith.

title: Does the Quran describe people being transformed into apes and pigs?
text: Describes a group among the Children of Israel who violated the Sabbath as being told "be apes, despised," and separately describes some as transformed into apes and pigs as a curse for disobedience.
note: Some modern commentators read this as describing moral or spiritual degradation (miskh, "metamorphosis") rather than literal physical transformation, and note the punished group is explicitly Sabbath-breakers, not Jews as a whole. Classical exegetes (Ibn Kathir, Ibn Abbas, and the historic majority reading) treat it as a literal historical transformation. Critics note that regardless of the literal/metaphorical question, the passage singles out a specific community for a uniquely degrading punishment among the Quran's disobedience narratives.

contested_wording.transliteration: kūnū qiradatan khāsi'īn
contested_wording.gloss: "be apes, despised"

contested_wording.transliteration: wa ja'ala minhumu al-qiradata wa al-khanāzīr
contested_wording.gloss: "and made of them apes and pigs"

title: Does the Quran call disbelievers "the worst of creatures"?
text: States that those who disbelieve among the People of the Scripture and the polytheists will be in the Fire of Hell forever, described as "the worst of creatures" — immediately followed by a parallel verse calling believers who do good "the best of creatures."
note: The paired structure (worst/best) is read by many commentators as a statement about the consequence of belief versus disbelief as a category, applied evenhandedly to any person based on their choice, rather than a claim about any specific ethnicity or group. Critics note the language is nonetheless categorical and severe, applied broadly to two named religious communities (Jews and Christians specifically named as "People of the Scripture") plus polytheists collectively, not narrowed to any specific historical dispute.

title: Does the Quran warn against close friendship with outsiders?
text: Instructs believers not to take intimates from outside their own community, stating that such people wish to see believers suffer and conceal hatred greater than what they openly show.
note: Classical commentators including al-Qurtubi read this as addressing a specific situation of active hostility and risk of betrayal (entrusting secrets or strategy to people working against the community's interest), not a blanket rule against ordinary friendship or courtesy with non-Muslims — citing other verses and hadith encouraging kindness to non-Muslims generally. Critics note the verse's own wording makes no explicit carve-out for this narrower reading, presenting a general claim about outsiders' concealed hatred.

title: Was Dhul-Qarnayn the pagan king Alexander the Great, recast as a monotheist?
text: Dhul-Qarnayn ("the Two-Horned One") travels to where the sun sets and rises, and builds an iron-and-copper wall against Gog and Magog — a narrative closely paralleling the pre-Islamic Syriac Alexander Legend, in which Alexander the Great does the same things in the same order, right down to the wall's construction materials.
note: Most Islamic and Western scholars identify Dhul-Qarnayn with Alexander the Great specifically because the parallels with the Syriac legend are too close and numerous to be coincidental — matching iconography ("two horns"), itinerary, and the Gog-and-Magog wall episode. The historical Alexander, however, was a documented pagan polytheist who styled himself the son of the god Zeus-Ammon and sought divine honors — starkly at odds with the pious monotheist believer depicted in the Quranic account. A minority of Muslim scholars reject the Alexander identification specifically because of this mismatch, some proposing alternative figures (Cyrus the Great, a pre-Islamic South Arabian king) instead, precisely to avoid attributing monotheistic piety to a historical pagan ruler.

title: Does the Quran describe a scientific barrier between fresh and salt water?
text: Describes God releasing two bodies of water, one fresh and one salty, with a barrier and "forbidding partition" between them that they do not cross.
note: A popular apologetic claim identifies this with the halocline effect at river-ocean estuaries, where density differences create a temporary boundary layer, framed as unknowable 7th-century knowledge. Critics raise two separate problems: first, the Arabic word used (bahr) means "sea" in classical usage, not "river" — the verse describes two seas meeting, not a river meeting an ocean, which doesn't match the estuary explanation apologists rely on; second, real estuary waters do eventually mix into brackish water rather than remaining permanently separated, which is at odds with the verse's language of a "forbidding" barrier that is never crossed.

contested_wording.transliteration: maraja al-baḥrayni yaltaqiyān, baynahumā barzakhun lā yabghiyān
contested_wording.arabic: مَرَجَ الْبَحْرَيْنِ يَلْتَقِيَانِ بَيْنَهُمَا بَرْزَخٌ لَّا يَبْغِيَانِ
contested_wording.gloss: "He released the two seas, meeting; between them is a barrier they do not transgress"

contested_wording.transliteration: hādhā 'adhbun furātun wa hādhā milḥun ujāj
contested_wording.arabic: هَٰذَا عَذْبٌ فُرَاتٌ وَهَٰذَا مِلْحٌ أُجَاجٌ
contested_wording.gloss: "this one fresh and sweet, and this one salty and bitter"

contested_wording.transliteration: wa ja'ala baynahumā ḥājizā
contested_wording.gloss: "and placed a barrier between them"

title: Does the Quran describe oceanographic internal waves and light attenuation in deep water?
text: Describes darkness in a deep sea, covered by wave upon wave, topped by clouds — layers of darkness so complete that a person could barely see their own hand.
note: Apologists connect this to the real oceanographic facts that light fades to near-total darkness below roughly 200 meters, and that internal waves exist at density boundaries deep underwater. The verse's own text undercuts the literal-scientific reading, though: it opens with an explicit simile marker ("or [the state of the disbelievers] is like...") introducing a metaphor for the spiritual darkness of unbelief, not a standalone description of ocean physics — a point classical tafsir treats as the verse's plain, primary meaning.

title: Does the Quran's grammar reveal that female bees do the foraging?
text: Describes God inspiring "the bee" to take dwellings in mountains, trees, and structures, then to eat from fruits and follow the ways laid down for it, using a feminine verb form.
note: Apologists point to the feminine grammatical verb form as evidence the text specifically identifies female worker bees as the foragers and builders — a real biological fact, since only female bees leave the hive to forage. Linguists counter that Arabic uses feminine verb forms for collective/species nouns (ism al-jins) regardless of the actual sex of individuals involved, pointing to parallel usage elsewhere in the same surah for birds (16:79) and for "the Romans" (30:2, clearly not referring to female Romans specifically) — meaning the grammar doesn't actually encode a claim about bee sex at all.

title: Does the Quran anticipate the forensic uniqueness of fingerprints?
text: Asks whether man thinks his bones will not be reassembled after death, answering that God is able to perfectly restore even the very tips of his fingers.
note: A popular modern claim reads "fingertips" as a specific reference to the forensic uniqueness of fingerprints, framed as unknowable 7th-century knowledge. The scientific understanding that every individual's fingerprints are unique wasn't established until Sir Francis Galton's work in the late 19th century, over 1,200 years after this text — and the verse's own context is about God's power to perfectly resurrect and reassemble the body in complete detail, using fingertips as an example of fine anatomical precision, not a claim about individual identification or forensics specifically.
